sentences.text: Ann Balfour came to the bookshop the next afternoon.
She was maybe fifty-five.
She had a warm coat and slightly worried eyes.
Rosa had laid the eleven books out on the counter.
Ann looked at them for a while without speaking.
Then she said, "Ah.
I did not know — I did not know these were in the house.
I did not go through the library carefully.
I just packed the books up and brought them here." She looked up.
"You want to know who did this.
Am I right." Rosa said, "Yes.
If you know."
Ann sighed.
She said, "I know.
It was my mother.
And her mother before her.
And her mother's mother before that.
Four generations of Balfour women — great-grandmother, grandmother, mother, and — very briefly — me.
Well, I stopped.
I could not do it.
But the three before me — yes.
They tore the endings out."
Iona and Rosa waited.
Ann settled herself.
She said, "It started with my great-grandmother, Elspeth Balfour.
She was born in 1856.
She was — from what my mother told me — a very serious woman.
She loved reading.
She read a great deal.
And one day, when she was maybe your age — she read a novel that had an ending she felt was — wrong.
She felt the author had — cheated.
Had put a false ending on a real story.
She was so angry that she tore the last chapter out.
She kept the book on her shelf without its ending.
It was a small — protest."
"And then — well.
She started thinking.
She realized she could do it whenever she wanted.
Whenever an ending felt wrong to her, she could just tear it out.
Not tell anyone.
And so — over her life — she tore the endings out of maybe thirty books.
Only the ones whose endings she felt were wrong.
Not all of them.
Some novels she felt ended honestly.
Those she left alone.
But the ones where she felt the author had let her down — she tore."
"When she was old," Ann went on, "she told her daughter, Mairi — my grandmother — what she had been doing.
Mairi took it up.
She continued.
And when Mairi was old she told her own daughter, Isla — my mother.
And my mother continued.
Sixty, seventy years, on and off.
All three of them tearing endings out of novels they thought had cheated them.
Only when they had been really disappointed.
Not out of spite.
Out of — a kind of principle.
As if they were correcting the historical record.
As if they were saying — this book will not be complete on my shelf, because it did not deserve completion."
"When my mother was old," said Ann, "she wanted to teach me.
I did try.
She gave me a novel one Christmas — I do not remember what it was — that she thought was going to make me want to tear the last chapter out.
She said — read it, and see how you feel.
I read it.
I did not want to tear the ending out.
I thought the ending was fine.
I told her.
She looked at me for a long time.
Then she said, — Ann, you are not one of us.
That is all right.
Not everyone is one of us.
Do not force it.
And she never asked me again."
Rosa said, "So it stopped with your mother." Ann said, "It stopped with my mother.
She was the last.
She was ninety-three when she died.
She had been tearing endings out on and off for eighty years.
If you count everything the three of them did, they must have — corrected — maybe eighty or ninety books, across the four generations.
I do not know where all of them are now.
Some my great-grandmother sold.
Some my grandmother gave away.
Angus bought some in the sixties.
Now you have the last of them." Ann looked at Iona.
"That is the whole story.
That is why the last chapters are gone from these books.
Because three women in my family thought the books had let them down.
That is all."
Iona said, quietly, "Miss Balfour.
What were the endings that they took away.
Do you know any of them.
What actually happened in the missing chapters." Ann smiled a small smile.
She said, "That is the interesting question.
I know some.
My mother knew some.
She had read the endings before she tore them out — that was the whole point, she had to read them to know if she wanted to tear them out.
She told me a few.
If you are interested, I could — I could write down what I remember.
I could send it to Rosa.
Would that be useful."
"Yes," said Rosa.
"That would be extraordinarily useful.
I want to make a small shelf.
Just for these books.
All eleven.
I want a small card explaining what happened to them.
Not so I can sell them — I won't sell them.
Just so people who visit the shop can see them, and can read the note, and can think about what it means.
If you would be willing to write down what you know about the missing endings — I would put your notes with the books." Ann nodded slowly.
She said, "I would like that.
I would like the tradition to be — remembered, at least.
Even if no one in my family is going to keep doing it."
That evening Rosa and Iona built the small shelf.
It was in the front corner of the shop, near the counter.
Rosa lettered a small card by hand: THE BALFOUR SHELF — BOOKS THAT WERE CORRECTED.
She wrote a longer note that explained the family history.
She put it on a small stand beside the shelf.
She put the eleven books on the shelf.
She did not put them for sale.
She put them for looking at.
The shelf stayed there for years.
Ann Balfour came back a few weeks later with a small notebook.
In it, she had written down what she remembered of the missing endings — five of the eleven books, she said, her mother had told her about, and she wrote down what her mother had said.
Some of the endings she remembered had been — unearned, her mother had said.
A character had been saved from a fate they had, in the story, clearly earned.
Others had been — falsely happy, tied up too neatly.
One had been — a marriage that made no sense given everything that had come before it.
Iona read all five accounts carefully.
She could see, in each case, why a very serious reader might have felt cheated.
She could not tell if the readers had been right or the authors had been right.
She thought — maybe both.
Maybe neither.
Maybe there was no answer.
For many years after that, Iona kept coming to the shop.
Rosa stayed until Iona was seventeen, and then Rosa moved to Edinburgh to run a bigger bookshop, and a new owner took over ByreBooks.
The Balfour Shelf stayed.
Every new owner kept it.
People visiting the town would sometimes discover it, and they would stand there for a long time, reading Ann's notes.
Some of them, Iona knew — because she had watched them — went home and started tearing the last chapters out of novels they thought had cheated them.
The tradition, in this small strange way, had not really died.
It had only moved.
That was what a small book town could do.
